name: Matrix Rain
basis: film's falling-code effect, animated per column (how)

lumenary.blurb: Falling code that glows brightest where your picture is bright.

facts.bestOn: High contrast pictures with a bright subject

why: The falling green characters are a visual idea about code made visible. Every column of this treatment has its own speed, trail and starting point, and the bright head of each drop leaves a fading trail. The picture appears because a drop glows brighter where the picture is brighter, and because bright regions hold a faint steady glow between drops.
how: Reduce the picture to one brightness value per character cell.
Give each column its own fall speed, trail length and offset, fixed by the seed.
Move the head of each drop down and fade the brightness along the trail behind it.
Make drops brighter where the picture is bright, and keep a faint glow in bright regions between drops.
Change characters at random, slowly in the trail and quickly at the head, and group them into ten brightness levels so painting stays fast.
history: The digital rain was designed for the 1999 film The Matrix by Simon Whiteley, who has said that the characters came from scans of Japanese cookbooks. It became shorthand for the idea of a hidden layer of code, and has been a screensaver, a meme and a tribute many times since.
uses: Title cards for talks and videos
terms: The shape of a single character.
The fading line of characters behind the head of a drop.
A function that turns inputs into pseudo-random but repeatable numbers.
paragraphs: The picture is reduced to one value per character cell. Each column has its own fall speed, trail length and starting offset, all fixed by the seed, so a column is a repeating drop. The head of a drop at time t is a position that moves down at that column’s speed and wraps round after it has left the bottom and its trail has gone. Behind the head the brightness falls off along the trail.

The picture shows through in two ways: a drop is brighter where the picture is brighter, and even between drops the bright parts of the picture hold a faint, constant glow of characters. The characters change at random, using a hash of the column, row and time, slowly in the trail and fast at the head. The head is drawn white with a glow. Characters are batched into ten brightness levels so that the program only changes the paint colour ten times a frame.

equations.note: Head position of column c in rows. r is the speed slider, s the column speed, o its offset, N the number of rows and ℓ the trail length.
Brightness of the character d rows behind the head. B is the picture brightness at the cell and σ the picture strength.

presets.text: Amber kana looks like a very old terminal.
Strong picture strength shows the portrait clearly.
Fast, tiny glyphs make a dense downpour.
